exercises.objective: Explain why the TD error's sign drives V(s) in the intuitively correct direction.
exercises.prompt: Explain, in terms of the TD error $r+\gamma V(s')-V(s)$, why receiving more reward than expected increases $V(s)$, and less reward than expected decreases it.
hints: $V(s)$ was our old estimate of the expected total future return from $s$; $r+\gamma V(s')$ is a fresh, one-sample re-estimate using what actually just happened.

If $r+\gamma V(s')>V(s)$ (more reward than the old estimate implied), the TD error is positive, so the update $V(s)\leftarrow V(s)+\alpha[\text{TD error}]$ increases $V(s)$, nudging it toward the better-than-expected outcome.

Symmetrically, if $r+\gamma V(s')<V(s)$, the TD error is negative and $V(s)$ decreases: the update always moves the old estimate a small step toward whatever was actually just observed, exactly why it's called 'reinforcement.'

exercises.objective: Derive Q-learning's update rule from the Bellman optimality equation for Q*.
exercises.prompt: Starting from RL-02's Bellman optimality equation $Q^*(s,a)=R(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a')$, derive Q-learning's update rule by replacing the exact expectation with a single sampled transition $(s,a,r,s')$.
hints: The exact Bellman equation requires summing over every possible $s'$, weighted by $P(s'\mid s,a)$; without a known model, replace this with the single $s'$ actually observed, and $R(s,a)$ with the single observed $r$: the resulting one-sample estimate of the right-hand side is $r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')$.
This one-sample estimate is noisy, so instead of overwriting $Q(s,a)$ entirely, take a small step of size $\alpha$ toward it, exactly like TD-learning's update for $V$.

$Q_\text{new}(s,a)=Q_\text{old}(s,a)+\alpha\big[r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q_\text{old}(s',a')-Q_\text{old}(s,a)\big]$: Q-learning's update, with $r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q_\text{old}(s',a')-Q_\text{old}(s,a)$ the TD error.

exercises.objective: Distinguish what TD-learning and Q-learning each estimate, regardless of the policy actually followed.
exercises.prompt: Explain precisely what TD-learning estimates versus what Q-learning estimates, and why Q-learning can use an exploratory ($\epsilon$-greedy) policy while still learning the *optimal* Q-function.
hints: TD-learning's update, $r+\gamma V(s')$, uses the *actual next action* $a=\pi(s)$ the policy took (implicitly, via whatever transition was observed under $\pi$): it estimates $V^\pi$, the value of the specific policy generating the data.

Q-learning's update instead uses $\max_{a'}Q(s',a')$, the *best possible* next action, regardless of what action was actually taken next: it estimates $Q^*$, the value of acting optimally from here on, no matter which policy generated the data used to learn it.

This is exactly why Q-learning tolerates (indeed needs) an exploratory, non-optimal behavior policy like $\epsilon$-greedy: since the target uses $\max_{a'}$ rather than the actually-taken action, the data-generating policy's own suboptimality never contaminates what's being learned, an important property called 'off-policy' learning.

exercises.prompt: For $r_t=2,\ r_{t+1}=3,\ \gamma=0.5$, and bootstrap estimate $V(s_{t+2})=10$, compute the 2-step return $R_t^{(2)}=r_t+\gamma r_{t+1}+\gamma^2V(s_{t+2})$. Enter a decimal.
hints: $R_t^{(2)}=2+1.5+2.5=6.0$. (Independently verified with Python while authoring this module.)
